slides.title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
slides.subtitle: This year you don't just learn new facts — you learn how to find them, like a young scientist.
points: Why is one side of a puri thinner than the other?
Are there more grains of sand on all the world's beaches, or more stars in our galaxy?
Why has nature created such a vast variety of plants and animals?

slides.title: Welcome back, investigators
slides.body: On the first page of every chapter you'll find a set of questions. These aren't meant for any exam — they are unique invitations to spark your curiosity and explore the world of science. Is there a question that makes you curious about the world? Write it down and carry it with you.

slides.title: The journey so far
slides.intro: Our journey with Curiosity continues into Grade 8. Let's see how far wonder has already carried us.

slides.title: Where we've been, where we're going
slides.body: Science began for you in **Grade 6** with wonder — the simple "Why?" and "How?" questions about everything around you. In **Grade 7** you saw that science keeps **evolving**: every answer you find opens up new questions. Now, in **Grade 8**, that wonder and that constant evolving come together as you step into the **Investigative World of Science** — where you don't just ask questions, you set out to find the answers yourself.

slides.title: Find new facts — don't just learn them
slides.body: We don't want you to just learn new facts; we want you to learn **how to find** new facts. Investigation means more than looking at something and asking simple questions. Now you can ask more **focused questions**, design **experiments** to answer them, and use your **observations** to improve your understanding.

slides.title: How a young scientist works
steps: Question — use a focused question as your starting point
Observe — look carefully with all your senses
Experiment — test it thoughtfully, changing one thing
Explain — make clear sense of what you saw

slides.title: The root and the kite
slides.leftBody: At the bottom of left-hand pages, a root — the deep, solid foundation of knowledge that keeps us connected to our environment, traditions, and natural heritage.
slides.rightBody: In the top corner of right-hand pages, a kite soaring in the sky — reminding us that curiosity must take flight if we are to explore the unknown.

slides.title: Solid roots, soaring ideas
slides.body: Together the root and the kite invite you to stay **grounded in real observations** while letting your ideas **soar towards new horizons**. Remember: investigation in science works best only when we balance the solid ground of careful observation with the freedom of **creative thinking**.

slides.title: This year's journey
slides.intro: From the tiny microbes we can't see to planet-wide challenges we can't ignore — let's preview the stops ahead.

slides.title: A hidden world in a drop of water
slides.body: We start by examining something as small as a single **drop of water**, uncovering a hidden world of tiny organisms. Some are **invisible helpers** that help us digest food or produce medicines, while others can be **harmful**, causing infections.

slides.title: How our body fights infection
slides.body: What does our body need to stay healthy, and how do we fight infections? We'll find out how **nutritious food**, exercise, **medicines**, and **vaccines** help us stay well. In today's world, science plays a major role in improving our lives.

slides.title: Heating and magnetic effects
slides.body: We use electric current in many ways to make life easier. We depend on the **heating effect** of electric current to keep us warm, while the **magnetic effect** helps motors and machines run and function.

slides.title: From a thrown ball to a cyclone
slides.body: These effects depend on fundamental **forces** — the things that make objects speed up, slow down, or change direction. Forces explain why a ball thrown up falls back, or why a car stops when you brake. This leads to **pressure**, which decides how air moves: a small difference brings a gentle breeze, a stronger one brings **winds and even cyclones**.

slides.title: Everything is made of tiny particles
slides.body: To understand how air exerts pressure or why water boils, we zoom into materials to see the **particles** they're made of. In **solids** these particles cannot move much, while in **gases** they move around freely. We then classify materials into **elements**, **compounds**, and **mixtures**.

slides.title: Dissolving sugar, bending light
slides.body: Once we know how particles combine or mix, we understand **solutions** — like how sugar dissolves in tea to make it sweet. From particles we move into the world of **light**: how it reflects off flat and curved mirrors, and **bends through lenses** — explaining the image in a shiny spoon or how glasses help us see clearly.

slides.title: Why the Moon changes shape
slides.body: It's not just polished mirrors that reflect light — rough surfaces do too, and so does the **Moon**. Depending on the relative positions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun, a slightly different part of the Moon is lit each night, giving rise to the beautiful **phases of the Moon** we see in the sky.

slides.title: Moon phases gave us calendars
slides.body: Watching the periodic cycles of the Moon's phases allowed humans to make the **first calendars**. By combining careful observations of sunrises, sunsets, and **lunar cycles**, various calendars came into being. Isn't it fascinating that the calendars guiding our routines on Earth are linked to objects far beyond our planet?

slides.title: Living things and their world
slides.body: There are marvellous, complex patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments. Every living being — from the tiniest insect to the largest whale, from blades of grass to tall trees — depends on the air, water, sunlight, and other organisms that form the **ecosystems** supporting life.

slides.title: What makes Earth 'just right'
slides.body: In the final chapter we put it all together. Earth lies at the perfect distance from the **Sun**, where water stays liquid, and has an **atmosphere** that gives us oxygen while shielding us from harmful rays. But human activities can change Earth's temperature, disrupting **climate** patterns. At the heart of both the problem and the solution — is us.

slides.title: Think like a scientist: the puri
slides.intro: Let's return to a question from the first page — why is one side of a puri thinner than the other? — and investigate it the way a scientist would.

slides.title: Your kitchen is a laboratory
slides.body: Science is everywhere — you don't need a fancy lab. Even your kitchen is a wonderful place to observe and ask **what happens if…?** Have you noticed how a **puri** or batura puffs up in hot oil, or how a phulka swells on the flame? Why does it puff like a balloon, and why is one side thinner than the other?

slides.title: What you change vs what you observe
slides.leftBody: Dough thickness · size of the rolled dough · type of flour (atta / maida) · oil temperature · how you drop it in (vertical / angled / slow)
slides.rightBody: Does it puff? (yes / no) · how long it takes to puff (seconds) · does a thick layer still give a thin side?

slides.title: Change only one thing at a time
slides.body: To make sense of the changes, it's better to change **only one thing** while keeping the other conditions the **same**. To see the effect of boiling-hot, hot, and not-very-hot oil, you'd use circles of dough of the same thickness, dropped in the same way.

slides.title: Investigate a puffing puri
slides.purpose: We want to find out **what makes a puri puff**, and why one side turns out thinner. So we ask a scientific question, then design simple experiments to test it — controlling some things and observing others.
steps: Question — what different things change the way a puri puffs?
Control — fix everything except the one thing you're testing (say, oil temperature)
Observe & measure — note if it puffs, time it in seconds, check for a thin side
Record — keep notes of all you sense: did the oil splatter, smell, or smoke?
slides.observe: Each round answers your question and **sparks new ones**: do puris puff better from fresh or stored dough? What happens if you prick a hole before frying? This is exactly how all scientific experiments are done — the idea of **systematic investigation**.

slides.title: Even a puri isn't fully understood
slides.body: Just so you know — even this simple everyday observation of a **puri puffing** is not completely understood by scientists today! Notice, note, and ask again: each careful observation feeds the next question. **This is how all science is done.**

slides.title: Where curiosity will take us
slides.body: From the tiniest microbe to the whole planet:

slides.transliteration: your guide for the journey ahead
slides.translation: The same scientific principles that guided us through the middle stages — observing, measuring, experimenting — will help us protect the delicate balance on which life depends. The challenges ahead won't always be easy, but we hope some of you will try to solve them.
slides.attribution: — Curiosity, Textbook of Science for Grade 8

slides.title: Happy investigating!
slides.subtitle: Whether it's the puffing of a puri or the shrinking bright part of the Moon after purnima, let your careful observations guide you into the investigative world of science.
